newsitem.title: USA: No CPI changes seen in U.S. FY98 budget proposal.
newsitem.headline: No CPI changes seen in U.S. FY98 budget proposal.

text.p: The White House is not likely to include any changes to the consumer price index (CPI) in its initial fiscal year 1998 budget proposal but the matter is likely to arise in later budget talks, White House spokesman Mike McCurry said on Wednesday.

"As a practical matter, given where we are in the budget cycle, it will not likely have immediate FY98 budget proposal consequences," McCurry said of the wide debate among academics and within Congress about changing the way CPI is measured.
But he suggested the matter will come up within budget negotiations between the White House and Congress next year.
"In the past this has been an issue that has arisen in bipartisan budget deliberations, and I suspect it will in the future," McCurry added.

A commission chaired by Stanford University economist Michael Boskin is scheduled to release a report today that is expected to argue that the CPI overstates inflation and that changes should be made to the way it is calculated.
Boskin said earlier Wednesday the commission would have recommendations for the president, Congress and the Bureau of Labor Statistics, including legislation, in its report.
But he declined to identify the recommendations and would also not confirm reports that the panel will declare that the CPI has an upward bias of 1.1 percent.
McCurry repeated the administration's position that it would weigh the commission's report, along with the views of other experts.

"We're committed to cost of living adjustments. We believe there may be some problems in measuring cost-of-living and we believe any changes in cost of living should be based on the best economic, scientific and technical analysis," he said.
"We are open to studying that type of analysis," McCurry added, declining to give any timeframe for how long it will take the administration to make up its mind on the matter.
The issue is critical for the budget process because of the indexing of social security payments and tax brackets.
